opus-5.5.text:
I think it came gradually, and a lot of it came from making mistakes rather than from someone telling me the answer.

Early on, like many students, I thought research meant finding a problem that looked hard and technically interesting, and then working very hard on it. Being diligent matters, but I slowly realized that how hard you work only multiplies whatever direction you've picked. If the direction is not that meaningful, even very good execution leads to something people don't really care about.

What changed my thinking was seeing which of my projects actually had an impact. When I worked on things like XGBoost, the original motivation wasn't "let me write a paper." It was that I saw a real gap. People wanted to use boosted trees on real data, and existing tools were either too slow or didn't scale. Because the problem was real, people started to use it, give feedback, and push it in directions I hadn't anticipated. That loop with real users taught me more than any single paper.

Later, working on deep learning systems and then compilers like TVM, I saw the same pattern. The interesting problems were at the boundaries: between machine learning and systems, between models and hardware. Those areas weren't crowded because they needed you to understand two communities at once. So I started asking myself a few questions before committing to a problem. Is this something that will matter in a few years, not just today? Is there a gap that I'm in a unique position to fill? And if it works, will someone actually use it?

I also learned that choosing a problem isn't a one-time decision. You start with a hypothesis about what's important, you build something, you see how the world reacts, and then you adjust. Sometimes the real problem turns out to be next to the one you started with.

So my advice to students now is to spend more time than feels comfortable thinking about what to work on. It's tempting to jump straight into execution because that feels productive. But a few extra weeks spent choosing the right problem can save years spent on the wrong one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts strong execution with choosing a meaningful research direction, but does not distinguish learning to solve predefined problems from learning to choose research problems.

r002.rationale: It describes learning through mistakes and projects such as XGBoost and TVM, but does not mention Professor Li Hang’s spam-detection talk as a turning point.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think it really goes back to my undergraduate years at Shanghai Jiao Tong, in the ACM class. When I started doing research, I was like most students: I would pick up whatever problem was in front of me, usually because a paper looked interesting or because a professor suggested it. I didn't really have a sense of what made a problem worth years of someone's life.

The shift happened in two stages. The first was around 2010, when I got involved in the KDD Cup and later the Netflix-style recommendation competitions. Competitions are brutally honest. You realize very quickly that most of the clever things you want to try don't matter, and the few things that do matter are often not the ones you expected. That taught me to ask, before starting anything, "If this works, who actually cares, and how much?"

The second stage was during my PhD at University of Washington with Carlos Guestrin. I remember him telling me that the hardest part of research is not solving the problem, it's choosing which problem to solve. At the time I was building what became XGBoost, and honestly it started as a side project for a competition. But I noticed something: people kept coming back to use it. Not because the algorithm was theoretically novel, but because it removed a real pain point. Gradient boosting existed; what didn't exist was a version that was fast, scalable, and reliable enough that a practitioner could trust it.

That was the moment it clicked for me. A good research problem sits at the intersection of three things. One, there's a genuine gap that many people are hitting, even if they can't articulate it. Two, the timing is right, meaning the surrounding technology has matured enough that a solution is possible now and not five years from now. And three, you personally have some unfair advantage, some combination of skills or perspective that makes you the right person to attack it.

Later, with MXNet and then TVM and MLC, I applied the same filter. For TVM, the question was: deep learning frameworks were multiplying, hardware was diversifying, and the gap between them, the compilation and deployment layer, was being handled by hand-written kernels. That was clearly unsustainable. The timing was right because the models were stabilizing enough to compile, and I had the background from both the systems side and the ML side.

So I'd say I came to understand it less from a single insight and more from repeatedly noticing which of my projects had impact and which quietly died. The ones that lived were always the ones where I had chosen the problem carefully, not the ones where I had the cleverest solution.

r001.rationale: He says he initially took on problems suggested by papers or professors, then learned to choose problems based on their importance and impact.

r002.rationale: He attributes the shift to competitions and PhD research; he does not mention Professor Li Hang’s talk on spam detection.

astra-6.text:
I think I came to appreciate it gradually. When you start doing research, you tend to focus on solving the problem in front of you: Can I make this algorithm better? Can I improve the performance? Those are important questions, but you also have to step back and ask why the problem matters and what solving it would enable.

One way I think about choosing problems is to ask who would care about the result. Would it remove a bottleneck for someone? Would it let people do something they couldn’t do before? Those questions help connect the technical challenge to a larger purpose.

And you don’t necessarily know the answer at the beginning. You need to explore, get feedback, and be willing to change direction. So choosing a problem is really part of the research process, rather than a decision you make once before the research starts.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts working on the problem already in front of you with stepping back to ask why it matters and choosing problems as part of research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Professor Li Hang’s spam detection talk or identify it as a turning point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it was a gradual realization. Early on, I focused a lot on how to solve a problem—learning the techniques, making an algorithm better, getting something to work. But you can spend a tremendous amount of effort solving a problem and still have very little impact if it isn’t the right problem to begin with.

That made me pay more attention to the question behind the work: Why does this matter? Who would benefit if we solved it? And is there something fundamental here that goes beyond this particular solution?

I still think you learn that judgment by doing research. You try things, see which ideas turn out to matter, and gradually develop a better sense of where to spend your time.

r001.rationale: It contrasts focusing on how to solve a problem with recognizing that choosing the right problem matters.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Professor Li Hang, a talk on spam detection, or that event as a turning point.
